analysis.one_liner: Gives banks permanent access to cheap Federal Reserve loans against underwater government bonds.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into law a permanent Federal Reserve lending program for banks, savings associations, and credit unions. Banks could borrow against U.S. government-guaranteed bonds for up to a year, with those bonds counted at full face value even if they are worth less on the market. It was introduced two months after the March 2023 bank failures and never moved in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, savings associations, and credit unions holding long-term Treasury or agency bonds that lost market value as interest rates rose. They could hand those bonds to the Fed and borrow their full face value at a fixed rate of the one-year swap rate plus 0.10%, with no fees and no prepayment penalty, avoiding selling the bonds at a loss.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a permanent Bank Term Funding Program under which Federal Reserve banks lend to insured banks, savings associations, credit unions, and U.S. branches of foreign banks for terms of up to one year, secured by collateral eligible for Fed open-market purchases — U.S. government-guaranteed securities, as the CRS summary describes.

Requires collateral to be valued at par with 100% margin, meaning a bank can borrow the full face value of a bond even if the bond currently sells for less on the market — letting the bank get cash without locking in a loss.
Sets the loan rate at a fixed one-year swap rate plus 10 basis points, charges no fee, and allows prepayment without penalty — cheap, flexible funding compared with selling assets into a weak market.

analysis.who_pays: The Federal Reserve, and ultimately taxpayers, bear the gap between face value and market value if a borrower defaults on an advance secured by depreciated bonds. More broadly, the public carries the risk of a permanent, no-fee backstop that encourages banks to keep holding long-term bonds funded by deposits that can flee quickly.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Federal Reserve and ultimately taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Valuing collateral at par with 100% margin means the Fed lends more than the security is worth on the market; if a bank cannot repay, the difference between face value and market value becomes a loss the Fed absorbs — although the advances are made with full recourse beyond the pledged collateral, so the Fed can pursue the borrower for the shortfall.

A permanent, fee-free facility with par valuation creates a standing incentive for banks to keep loading up on long-term bonds funded by flighty deposits, knowing a Fed lifeline exists if rates move against them — the same interest-rate mismatch that sank Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023.
The bill sets no cap on total lending and no sunset, making an emergency-style program a routine part of bank funding rather than a crisis tool.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the banking industry this would have been a valuable permanent subsidy: full face value against bonds the market prices lower, at a near-market rate with no fees. For everyone else the benefits are indirect at best — crisis loans could reduce fire sales of Treasury bonds — while the costs are the Fed absorbing the difference between face and market value when borrowers fail, plus a standing invitation for banks to take more interest-rate risk. The full-recourse feature limits the direct fiscal exposure, but the par-valuation and no-fee design are what make the program a subsidy rather than ordinary lending.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Financial Services Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer introduced the bill on May 11, 2023, two months after the March 2023 bank failures, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
Not a single member of the House from either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — and the bill never reached the House floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks did not get the permanent lending program, and the Federal Reserve and taxpayers were spared a new standing backstop for bank bond losses. Because the real emergency Bank Term Funding Program the bill echoed was always temporary, the status quo — a Fed that lends against collateral at market value through the discount window — remained in place.

for.name: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make a permanent bank lending facility part of the Federal Reserve Act.

against.name: Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the complete action history shows nothing after the initial referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so partisan positions were never tested.

industries.industry: Banks, savings associations, and credit unions
industries.note: The bill would have given depository institutions a permanent source of one-year Fed loans at full face value against government-guaranteed bonds worth less on the market, with no fees — a way to avoid realizing losses on interest-rate bets. The industry's gain would come from the Fed (and ultimately taxpayers) absorbing the difference, so the bill's interest runs against the public's.

The bill would hard-wire a new lending mandate into the Federal Reserve Act, expanding the Fed's role as a standing lender to banks against long-term assets. The Fed would gain a crisis tool but take on the par-valuation subsidy and the moral hazard that comes with a permanent backstop.
